Evolutionary strategies (CMA-ES, xNES) and finite-difference gradient approximation (FDSA, SPSA) are what the MATSim/eqasim calibration framework boptx implements. The cross-entropy method is a Monte-Carlo importance-sampling search and is the most expensive family: one published SUMO calibration of a three-intersection model spent 98,304 simulation evaluations. Bayesian optimisation over a surrogate is the current answer for a small budget (see the surrogate row). The field states its own constraint plainly: computational budgets in the literature are 'one to two orders of magnitude lower than the problem dimension', and general-purpose algorithms 'are designed for asymptotic performance guarantees and are not designed to be terminated with such few function evaluations'.
factors.magnitude: literature: a metropolitan-scale calibration is practically bounded at 10^1-10^3 simulation evaluations; a method needing 10^4+ is unreachable when one evaluation is a multi-hour run
factors.evaluations_required: SPSA: 2 simulation evaluations per gradient step, and visibly NOT converged after 15 on a 30,000-dimension problem. CMA-ES / xNES: population x generations, tens to hundreds. Cross-entropy: 98,304 in one published three-intersection SUMO case. Bayesian optimisation with a surrogate: 150-500 (see the surrogate row). Coordinate descent / grid: (points per parameter) x (free parameters) x (rounds).
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: eqasim and MATSim scenarios calibrate through boptx (CMA-ES, xNES, FDSA, SPSA, opdyts acceleration); SimMobility MT through Bayesian optimisation with a random-forest surrogate; ActivitySim and CT-RAMP through an iterative alternative-specific-constant adjustment rather than a general optimiser; SUMO through Cadyts, SPSA and cross-entropy.
factors.query: A head-to-head comparison of CMA-ES, Bayesian optimisation and coordinate descent on a MULTIMODAL MATSim scenario reporting simulation runs to reach a stated per-mode tolerance - the Hoerl accelerated-evolutionary-search paper (hal-03676897) was the target this pass and both HAL routes failed (access denied, then socket hang-up); try the boptx paper on arXiv or the MUM proceedings instead.

factors.what_research_says: The canonical line is Osorio's metamodel simulation-based optimisation: replace the expensive simulated objective with an analytical network model plus a low-order statistical correction, then solve a sequence of cheap analytical problems, so that good points are found from the first iterations without a large initial sample. Its strongest published demonstration is a Salt Lake City origin-destination calibration of order thirty thousand dimensions, where within ONE simulation iteration the linear-metamodel method took the vehicle-count nRMSE from 120% to 32%, against 48% for a tailored linear-assignment method and 117% for SPSA, all inside a fifteen-simulation-iteration budget - and 'thereafter there is not much improvement within such few iterations', i.e. nearly all the gain arrives at the first evaluation. The second family is machine-learned rather than analytical: a random-forest surrogate driving Bayesian optimisation calibrated 477 behavioural parameters of the SimMobility MT activity-based model for Tallinn, and did so against AGGREGATE benchmarks ('the modal share of the whole population'), reaching 4% error on the total number of trips and an average origin-destination error of 15.92 vehicles per day. That paper states no prior work had calibrated as many as 477 parameters and that existing rigorous methods 'do not consider more than a few dozen of parameters (the maximum number being 98)'.
factors.magnitude: literature: a surrogate converts a calibration from thousands of simulation evaluations to order 1-500; the analytical metamodel reached its best point in ONE simulation iteration and the random-forest/Bayesian surrogate in 'slightly more than 150'
factors.evaluations_required: Analytical linear metamodel: a substantially improved point after 1 simulation iteration; benchmark run to 15. Random-forest surrogate + Bayesian optimisation: best solution after 'slightly more than 150 iterations', termination set at '500 iterations or 500 hours', where one SimMobility Preday evaluation over ~400,000 individuals costs 6-8 hours on a laptop.
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Osorio's metamodel framework is applied to signal control, congestion pricing, car-sharing fleet assignment and toll optimisation on microscopic simulators; SimMobility MT (Tallinn) uses a random-forest surrogate under Bayesian optimisation; no public MATSim scenario calibrates through a surrogate - the MATSim family runs black-box search (boptx) or an ASC adjustment loop instead.
factors.query: A surrogate-assisted calibration of a MULTIMODAL agent-based model whose targets are per-mode ridership rather than link counts or an OD matrix - Osorio's 2020 metamodel-based calibration of large-scale multimodal microscopic traffic simulation (S0968090X20307592) is the obvious candidate and is paywalled; try an author preprint on web.mit.edu/osorioc.

factors.what_research_says: A parameter set is identified only if distinct parameter values produce distinguishable outputs on the targets you actually hold, and the simulation-calibration literature is explicit that when a model is over-parametrised relative to its targets, 'non-identifiability can arise, making it theoretically impossible to locate the true parameter value'. The published remedy is not a better optimiser but a different answer: report an ELIGIBILITY SET - the set of all parameter values whose simulated outputs match the data - constructed to carry rigorous frequentist guarantees, extended to multivariate outputs by a feature-extraction-then-aggregation construction. The counting rule underneath is what binds a mode-share calibration: K shares that sum to one contain K-1 independent numbers, so scoring twelve modelled modes against a five-mode survey does not supply twelve independent targets. The only way to buy identifiability for more parameters is to add targets of a DIFFERENT kind - link counts, boardings, trip-length and duration distributions - not more shares of the same total. The OD-calibration literature reaches the same place from the other side: 'the problem is underdetermined ... there are typically an infinite number of vectors x that can reproduce these counts', which is why a regularisation term toward a prior seed matrix is standard.
factors.magnitude: literature: identifiability is counted in independent numbers, not in printed targets; an over-parametrised calibration has no point answer at all, only a set
factors.evaluations_required: not an evaluation count: the eligibility-set construction is a statistical guarantee over whatever evaluations the search made, not a budget
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim and CT-RAMP sidestep the question by moving only the mode constants, one per mode, against one share per mode; the OD-calibration literature adds an explicit regularisation term toward a prior seed matrix; no public agent-based transport model reports an eligibility set or a confidence region over its behavioural parameters.
factors.query: A transport-specific treatment of set-valued calibration (eligibility sets or confidence regions over behavioural parameters) rather than a point estimate - none found this pass; enter through the ACM TOMACS 2025 eligibility-set paper's transport citations.

factors.factor: Estimating choice parameters from aggregate data only
factors.what_research_says: Three distinct families exist for a city with no unit-record survey. (1) AGGREGATE ASC ADJUSTMENT, the practice standard: iteratively add the log ratio of observed to modelled share to each mode constant, re-run, repeat until the split is inside a stated threshold, commonly plus or minus one percentage point; ActivitySim adjusts tour-level and trip-level constants together with the same increment because tour mode conditions trip mode. The profession's own validation manual warns that revising constants is 'a last resort' after other checks are exhausted, because a constant absorbs every omitted variable. (2) BLP-STYLE DEMAND INVERSION: a contraction mapping inverts observed market shares to implied mean utilities and GMM on instrumented moments recovers heterogeneous taste coefficients 'from only aggregate market-share data', removing the IIA restriction on substitution; the requirement is instruments with genuine cross-market variation, which a single-city model does not naturally possess. (3) SURROGATE-ASSISTED SIMULATION-BASED ESTIMATION against aggregate benchmarks: the Tallinn SimMobility work fitted 477 behavioural parameters entirely against 'aggregate benchmarks (e.g., the modal share of the whole population)' and names disaggregate data only as future work - a direct feasibility proof that unit records are not a precondition for fitting a large behavioural parameter set.
factors.magnitude: literature: aggregate-only estimation is feasible and standard; the practice acceptance tolerance is about plus or minus one percentage point on mode share, and the ceiling is that a constant absorbs whatever the utility omits
factors.evaluations_required: Aggregate ASC adjustment: one simulation run per adjustment round, typically a handful of rounds to reach a one-percentage-point threshold. BLP inversion: no simulation runs at all - it is estimated outside the simulator, on the share table. Surrogate-assisted: 150-500 (row I8).
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim and CT-RAMP run the iterative ASC adjustment to a stated threshold; eqasim calibrates mode-specific constants through boptx to fit overall mode shares; Rakow and Nagel's automated ASC calibration is the MATSim-native version; the industrial-organisation literature runs BLP on share data alone; MATSim scenarios in general import coefficients estimated elsewhere on unit records and adjust only the constants locally.
factors.query: A transport application of BLP-style share inversion to MODE shares, with zones or time periods as the markets and the instruments named - the search returned only industrial-organisation applications this pass.

factors.what_research_says: Population synthesis is the required input to any agent model because individual-level attributes for the whole population do not exist; the established techniques are iterative proportional fitting, iterative proportional updating, combinatorial optimisation, and Markov- and fitness-based synthesis. There is no clear guideline on choosing among them, and integer conversion and the zero-cell problem are the outstanding issues.
factors.magnitude: literature: IPF/IPU/combinatorial optimisation/Markov the established families; no consensus on choice; integer conversion and zero cells the open problems
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim ships PopulationSim; MATSim scenarios use eqasim's synthesiser or a bespoke one; every platform in the survey treats the synthetic population as an input rather than a modelled object.
factors.query: J Population synthesis: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Household travel survey estimates are produced on a rolling basis from multiple pooled years and weighted to the ABS Estimated Resident Population for the collection year - so an HTS figure is a multi-year average, not a single-year observation. The survey's known systematic weakness is the undercount of short walk trips: every national survey from 1977 to 2022 has undercounted total walk trips by omitting short walks to stops and car parks.
factors.magnitude: literature: HTS estimates are rolling multi-year pooled and ERP-weighted; walk trips systematically undercounted in every survey series examined
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Every activity-based model in the field calibrates against an HTS of this kind; the vintage-versus-base-year mismatch is universal and rarely stated.
factors.query: J Travel survey (HTS) weighting and vintage: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Smartcard data is the standard calibration source for transit and it supports high-quality validation - agent-based models calibrated on it reach R-squared around 0.85 on on-board bus volumes - but it is structurally incomplete: most datasets capture only entry and egress points with no routing information, so trip-chaining is required to infer alighting stops and identify transfers.
factors.magnitude: literature: smartcard-calibrated transit ABMs reach R^2 ~0.85 on on-board volumes; alighting and transfers must be inferred by trip-chaining
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Visum, Emme and MATSim scenarios all calibrate PT to smartcard boardings where available; per-station validation for every mode is uncommon.
factors.query: J Smartcard (Opal) and station counts: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Traffic counts are not a fixed truth: counts alone vary by 10% or more from daily and seasonal variation, and FHWA recommends a minimum of one midweek 24-hour count at least every two years to obtain a typical ADT estimate. Validation percentages are therefore reported by functional class and against screenlines rather than link by link.
factors.magnitude: literature: >=10% intrinsic variability in count data; validation reported by functional class and screenline, not per link
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Every four-step and ABM practice validates on counts; MATSim scenarios in the literature report link-count scatter as the primary validation.
factors.query: J Road counts: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: OpenStreetMap road completeness is about 83% globally (Barrington-Leigh and Millard-Ball 2017) and highest in cities; a 41,000 km Australian road network study finds OSM navigation performance correlates strongly with data quality, which itself tracks city population and ICT infrastructure. GTFS is the interoperable timetable format because timetables change too often for OSM; the join between the two (pt2matsim here) is the recurring failure point.
factors.magnitude: literature: OSM roads ~83% complete globally, higher in cities; Australian OSM quality tracks population and ICT
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: pt2matsim, OpenTripPlanner and UrbanAccess join GTFS to OSM; validators (gtfs-validator) check feed integrity but not map completeness.
factors.query: OSM completeness for the Hunter region against the TfNSW road segment layer (km matched)

factors.what_research_says: Downscaling has measured limits: simulations at 25% or higher of the traveller population preserve all major urban traffic statistics, while below 10% even average statistics become unreliable, with scores and travel times the first to degrade. The scaling rule is that flowCapacityFactor follows the sample share and storageCapacityFactor is set a little higher at samples of 10% or below; in one published scenario a 1% population needed a 2% flow capacity factor to reproduce the observed travel-distance distribution.
factors.magnitude: literature: >=25% preserves all major traffic statistics; below 10% even averages are unreliable; storage capacity factor set above flow at small samples
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim, SUMO and BEAM all scale link capacities with the sample; the field's usual practice is 1-10%, and 25% is at the high end of published scenarios.
factors.query: K Sample fraction and scaling rules: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: There is no standard iteration count: the process is run until the average population score stabilises, simple car-only scenarios converge fast, complex multimodal ones sometimes do not converge by iteration 100, one published scenario converged at iteration 164 and others run 500; because the simulation is stochastic, deterministic convergence criteria do not apply.
factors.magnitude: literature: 100-500 iterations in published scenarios; one converged at 164; no multimodal twelve-mode benchmark
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Published MATSim scenarios commonly run 100-500 iterations with an innovation-off tail; eqasim and BEAM likewise.
factors.query: Iteration counts and post-cutoff windows reported by multimodal MATSim city scenarios with PT and active modes

factors.what_research_says: Run-to-run reproducibility is not achievable by fixing a seed alone in this class of model: across 100 seeds relative errors up to 10% occur on high-volume links, and between-seed variation dominates the last-two-iteration within-seed variation. Reporting a single seeded run is therefore reporting one draw from a distribution.
factors.magnitude: literature: up to 10% relative link-volume error across seeds; between-seed variation dominates within-seed
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Aimsun and Vissim require multiple replications; most published MATSim scenarios report one seed and do not state the noise floor.
factors.query: K Reproducibility of a run: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.factor: Sequential versus simultaneous calibration of many targets
factors.what_research_says: The field states the choice explicitly and it is a real fork, not a matter of taste. In dynamic OD calibration, 'the first formulation estimates the whole set of time-dependent OD matrices SIMULTANEOUSLY for the entire time period in one calibration round. The second formulation estimates and calibrates OD matrices SEQUENTIALLY one at a time for each time frame. Most optimization-based studies have used the simultaneous approach, since the available sequential methods may lose accuracy due to giving up some information in the transition between time frames' - while the simultaneous form 'is incapable of handling a stream of data for real-time or online demand calibration'. The same paper states the bind that makes the choice matter at all: 'this optimization problem is underdetermined for large-scale networks since the number of roads with traffic measurement is usually several orders of magnitude smaller than the number of all roads in the network', and it names the standard architecture as BI-LEVEL - an upper-level discrepancy minimisation over an inner assignment that must be re-solved at every candidate, where 'performing several DTAs for each optimization task demand considerable computational resources'. In DTA practice the sequential form is supply first and then demand with the supply held fixed; the reported weakness of decomposing is that the stages need not be internally consistent, because each stage's assumed input is not the other stage's output.
factors.magnitude: literature: no numeric tolerance - a structural statement. Simultaneous calibration is the majority practice and the one that keeps the stages consistent; sequential decomposition buys tractability and streaming at the cost of the information lost between stages
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: DTA practice (Ben-Akiva / Balakrishna) calibrates supply first and demand second by default, with simultaneous demand-and-supply estimation as the published improvement; ActivitySim and CT-RAMP calibrate component by component down the model chain (long-term, tour, trip) and move tour and trip constants together only because tour mode conditions trip mode; the MATSim ASC loops move every open constant in one round.
factors.query: A head-to-head on a MULTIMODAL agent-based model of moving every mode constant in one round against moving them one mode at a time, reporting simulation runs to a stated per-mode tolerance.

factors.factor: Damping and step-size schedule in the constant-adjustment contraction
factors.what_research_says: The log-ratio ASC step is a contraction only if it is damped, and the two open implementations of it disagree on how. The leading open MATSim calibrator, matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools, computes the raw step verbatim as 'math.log(z_i) - math.log(m_i) - (math.log(z_0) - math.log(m_0))' and applies it under a SCHEDULE whose default is 'linear_scheduler(start=0.6, end=1, interval=3)' - the early rounds take 0.6 of the raw step and the fraction relaxes to the full step over three intervals, i.e. cautious while the shares are far from target and undamped once they are near. The agency practice in the ActivitySim world applies a FLAT dampener instead of a schedule. Neither publishes a convergence proof, and the same library's 'TerminationCondition.check_termination' still carries '# TODO: not used yet' - so the field's standard answer ships a damping default and no working stopping rule at all. The undamped step (1.0) is the boundary case: it is what a fixed point converges to when it converges, and what overshoots when the shares are far out.
factors.magnitude: literature: damping about 0.5-0.6 of the raw log-ratio step at the start, relaxed toward 1.0 over roughly three rounds (the matsim-vsp default); a flat 0.5 in the ActivitySim agency practice. No published convergence rate for either.
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools schedules the step with linear_scheduler(0.6 -> 1 over 3 intervals) under Optuna; ActivitySim / CT-RAMP practice uses a flat dampener on the same ln(observed/modelled) increment; eqasim's boptx runs a general optimiser instead and has no damping parameter of this kind; Cadyts adjusts no parameter at all and so has no step to damp.
factors.query: A published convergence or oscillation study of the damped ln(observed/modelled) ASC update on a MULTIMODAL agent-based model - round-over-round |delta| against the damping factor. Nothing found this pass beyond the two implementations' shipped defaults.

factors.factor: Diagnosing a residual: constant versus missing mechanism
factors.what_research_says: The profession's own manual puts constant adjustment LAST and lists what must be exhausted first. FHWA's Travel Model Validation and Reasonableness Checking Manual, chapter 7 (Mode Choice / Vehicle Occupancy), states that 'simple adjustments to modal constants estimated using weighted samples should be considered "a last resort" after all other possible causes for error and calibration adjustments have been considered', and its Table 7.6 orders the checks ahead of it: verify trip distribution for the market segment, check that the implied transit share is reasonable, recheck the skim data (networks, time periods, geographic scope), consider revising the model STRUCTURE, evaluate indicator variables or adjust their coefficients - and only then revise an alternative-specific constant. The same chapter states plainly that 'there are no applicable criteria guidelines for checks of mode choice', so the field supplies an ORDER of diagnosis and no numeric bar. What it does not supply anywhere reached this pass is a TEST that separates the two cases: no source reviewed proposes reading the round-over-round behaviour of the constant update itself as the diagnostic.
factors.magnitude: literature: an ORDERED CHECKLIST, not a coefficient - five classes of check ahead of any constant revision, and no numeric acceptance criterion for mode choice at all
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: US MPO practice follows the manual's order and records the checks in a calibration report; MATSim and eqasim scenarios in the published literature adjust the constants against reference shares without reporting a preceding diagnosis; no surveyed project publishes a test that separates a taste residual from a missing mechanism.
factors.query: A published TEST (not a checklist) that distinguishes a residual an alternative-specific constant can legitimately absorb from one caused by an absent mechanism - for instance reading the contraction behaviour of the ASC update over successive rounds. None found this pass.

factors.factor: Multi-objective aggregation across many simultaneous targets
factors.what_research_says: Aggregating many targets into one number has a known and specific failure. Jakob and Blume set it out: with a weighted sum, 'by varying the weights, any point of a convex Pareto front can be obtained... On the other hand, it is possible that parts of the Pareto front cannot be found in case of a non-convex problem... the part between points A and B of the Pareto front cannot be obtained for any weights. This is a serious drawback.' The counterweight is cost: 'the computational effort to determine all or at least most of the Pareto front increases significantly with the number of conflicting objectives', and the paper's framing is that the real-world question arises 'where either more than four objectives have to be considered, or the same type of task is repeated again and again with only minor modifications'. So beyond about four conflicting targets a full Pareto treatment is expensive and scalarisation is the practical route - while the scalarisation chosen decides which compromises are reachable at all. A weighted sum of squared deviations across targets is the standard form in simulation-based transport calibration.
factors.magnitude: literature: a weighted sum cannot reach the non-convex parts of a Pareto front for ANY weights; Pareto methods' cost rises sharply past about four conflicting objectives
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: SPSA-family and boptx calibrations minimise a weighted sum of squared deviations across targets; the SimMobility MT surrogate work aggregates aggregate benchmarks into one objective; the ABM literature recommends evolutionary multi-objective optimisation with a Pareto set where the trade-offs must be seen. Whether a MIN-MAX / Chebyshev scalarisation over the targets escapes the non-convexity limitation is NOT stated by this source and was not verified this pass - it is recorded as a gap, not asserted.
factors.query: Whether a MIN-MAX (Chebyshev / worst-target) scalarisation reaches Pareto points a weighted sum cannot, stated in a transport-calibration source - and any transport application that reports a Pareto set over per-mode deviations rather than one aggregated number.

factors.factor: Router-scorer consistency: does the search optimise the utility the plan is scored by?
factors.what_research_says: MATSim's own choice-model chapter makes the split explicit: an agent's realised behaviour is P(i|U) = sum over choice sets of P(i|C) x P(C|U) - the choice model AND the way the choice set was generated. The router is the choice-set generator, so a router that optimises a different objective from the scoring function generates alternatives the scorer will then reject, and 'alternatives that never appear in the choice set cannot be chosen'. MATSim's stock car routing keeps the two aligned by deriving the link travel cost from the scoring parameters (the negative marginal utility of travelling plus the marginal utility of performing); the alignment is deliberate and is broken wherever a specialised router is used. The SwissRailRaptor's DefaultRaptorInVehicleCostCalculator prices a boarded leg as in-vehicle seconds times one coefficient, so a per-submode constant, a fare or a crowding surcharge that lives only in scoring is invisible to the transit search that picks the submode.
factors.magnitude: literature: no coefficient - a structural identity. The realised choice distribution is the product of the choice model and the choice-set generator, so any objective the generator does not carry can only act by rejecting alternatives after they are built
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim core derives the car router's disutility from the scoring parameters; eqasim and the discrete-mode-choice contrib move the whole decision into an explicit choice model evaluated over an enumerated set, which removes the split; ActivitySim/CT-RAMP evaluate skims that are by construction the same quantities the utility uses; SUMO and Aimsun route on a generalised cost that is the objective.
factors.query: A measured effect on mode share of aligning versus not aligning a MATSim transit router's in-vehicle cost with the scoring function's mode constant

factors.factor: Equilibrium selection and the innovation cutoff: what the reported share is a share OF
factors.what_research_says: MATSim's iterative loop is not stationary while innovation runs: its own terminology page states that 'as long as innovation is still switched on in MATSim (new routes, new times, ...), the result is not truly stationary', and that once innovation is disabled 'the result is indeed a stationary process, but limited to the set of plans that every agent has at that point in time'. The selection protocol before the cutoff 'resembles a MNL choice model', P(i|C) = exp(mu S_i)/sum exp(mu S_j) with mu = brainExpBeta, and the chapter notes that BestPlanSelector is the same selector with an infinite mu. So the pre-cutoff share is a logit-dispersed mixture over each agent's remembered plans and the post-cutoff share is the same population collapsed toward its arg-max: switching innovation off changes the estimator, not only the amount of search. Assignment theory says the same thing from the other side - a low dispersion parameter concentrates flow on the perceived-best alternative and the pattern approaches deterministic user equilibrium, which is the classic 'unrealistic route concentration' that stochastic user equilibrium was introduced to cure. The efficiency loss of that concentration is bounded and modest on real networks - a data-driven estimate for Eastern Massachusetts puts the price of anarchy near 1.30, and other empirical work finds it close to 1 in both light and heavy traffic - so an equilibrium being reached is no guarantee that it resembles the observed day, which is itself a non-equilibrium average.
factors.magnitude: literature: the post-cutoff state is stationary but confined to the plans already held; selection is a logit at mu = brainExpBeta before the cutoff and effectively arg-max after it. Empirical price of anarchy about 1.30 (Eastern Massachusetts) and near 1.0 in light and heavy traffic - the equilibrium's inefficiency is bounded, its distance from an observed day is not
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim exposes fractionOfIterationsToDisableInnovation and fractionOfIterationsToStartScoreMSA and the field's usual setting is about 0.8; SUMO and Aimsun stop on an explicit relative gap rather than by disabling search; static four-step models solve a stochastic user equilibrium whose dispersion parameter is calibrated, so the spread is a fitted quantity rather than a by-product of when search was turned off; ActivitySim has no network equilibrium of its own.
factors.query: A published measurement of the mode-share step at the innovation cutoff in a multimodal MATSim scenario, and whether the pre-cutoff or post-cutoff share is the one validated against observation

factors.factor: Choice-set coverage as a binding constraint on any constant or price
factors.what_research_says: Flotterod and Kickhofer state the mechanism in one line and it is an identity, not a tendency: 'the generation of the choice sets affects the simulated choices. The simplest illustration of this mechanism is that alternatives that never appear in the choice set cannot be chosen. Similarly, including certain alternatives with a low (high) probability in the choice set decreases (increases) their probability of being chosen, given that the choice model is not changed.' They add the consequence for a calibration exercise directly: 'When a choice study's synthetic choice sets are very different from the alternatives considered in the real world, it is unlikely that the simulation will display correct aggregated quantities or useful sensitivities for policy measures', and that MATSim's mutation and innovation procedures 'constitute concrete, yet heuristic, approaches to the choice set generation problem' whose biases 'can, however, be difficult to quantify'. The plan memory is the other half of the constraint: the choice set is bounded by maxAgentPlanMemorySize, plans past it are deleted by a PlanSelectorForRemoval, and the MATSim user guide records that 'a problem is that the process that generates the choice set at this point is not systematic'. A mode constant therefore has an upper bound on what it can move that is set by the fraction of agents who ever held that mode in memory, not by its own magnitude.
factors.magnitude: literature: an alternative absent from an agent's set has probability zero for that agent regardless of its utility, so the reachable share of mode m is bounded above by the fraction of agents whose plan memory has ever contained m; MATSim's choice-set generation is explicitly heuristic and its bias is stated to be hard to quantify
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: The discrete-mode-choice contrib and eqasim replace on-the-fly innovation with an explicit, enumerated choice set per trip or tour, which makes coverage 100 per cent by construction; ActivitySim/CT-RAMP enumerate every alternative in a nested logit; MATSim core offers diversity-increasing replanning modules and path-size-logit-style corrections, described in the same chapter as 'ad-hoc solutions, with little theoretical foundation in the simulation context'.
factors.query: A published coverage figure - the fraction of agents that ever held a given mode in plan memory - for a calibrated multimodal MATSim scenario, and any guidance on a minimum coverage before a mode constant is calibrated. modeChoiceCoverage is undocumented outside the source

factors.factor: Mode availability by distance: an upper bound on a walk or bike alternative
factors.what_research_says: Cycling distance is short and its distribution is well measured. Australian travel survey data for 2012-2020 put the median home-based cycling trip at 3.5 km, varying strongly by purpose - 1.8 km utilitarian, 5.3 km commuting, 3.7 km recreational - with trip purpose the strongest predictor and men cycling further than women. The Montreal metropolitan survey puts the 85th percentile of cycling distance at 5,517 m, and the 85th-percentile access distance is the field's usual way of setting a catchment. Distance decay for cycling fits an exponential or lognormal curve rather than a cliff, so the correct representation is a decaying utility rather than a hard cut-off - but a simulator that offers the mode at any distance with no decay term places mass far out in a tail the survey does not contain.
factors.magnitude: literature: median home-based cycling trip 3.5 km (Australia, 2012-2020); 1.8 km utilitarian, 5.3 km commuting, 3.7 km recreational; 85th percentile 5.5 km (Montreal). Distance decay exponential or lognormal, not a cut-off
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: The discrete-mode-choice contrib ships explicit availability filters, including maximum-distance constraints per mode, as a first-class configuration; ActivitySim/CT-RAMP apply availability rules plus a distance term in the mode utility; MATSim core's SubtourModeChoice applies no distance test at all - a mode is offered wherever the chain-based resource rule allows it.
factors.query: Whether an agent-based model that adds a maximum-distance availability filter for bike and walk reports a measured change in those modes' shares, and what threshold was used

factors.factor: Distributional targets beyond mode share: trip length, intrazonal share, occupancy
factors.what_research_says: The profession does not accept a mode share as a model's validation on its own; it validates the distribution the share is drawn from. The standing guidance is explicit and numeric: 'Generally, the modeled average trip lengths for each trip purpose should be within five percent of observed for each trip purpose'; the trip length frequency distribution is compared as a whole using the coincidence ratio - 'the area under both curves divided by the area under at least one of the curves' - and 'it is preferable for the coincidence ratio for each trip purpose to be at least 70 percent'; and 'regionwide intrazonal trip percentages should be within three percentage points of observed for each trip purpose'. Vehicle occupancy has moved into the same class: in trip-based models the vehicle occupancy factor was an input converting person trips to vehicle trips, while 'in activity-based models (ABM), the role of VOF transitioned from a major input to a validation target for shared-rides'. On the assignment side the same manuals give volume tolerances by facility class - Ohio's VMT guidance is plus or minus 7 per cent on freeways and expressways, 10 per cent on principal and minor arterials, 15 per cent on collectors, with Michigan DOT at 5 and 10 per cent for screenlines and cutlines and Florida at 20 per cent for transit screenlines - while stating that 'the guidelines in this section should not be construed as standards'.
factors.magnitude: literature: mean trip length within 5 per cent of observed by purpose; trip-length-frequency coincidence ratio at least 70 per cent; intrazonal share within 3 percentage points; VMT within 7-15 per cent by facility class; screenline 5 per cent, cutline 10 per cent, transit screenline 20 per cent; vehicle occupancy a validation target in an activity-based model rather than an input
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Every four-step and activity-based practice model in the FHWA/TMIP tradition reports trip length distributions by purpose and a coincidence ratio alongside shares; ActivitySim calibration reports carry TLFD plots per purpose; published MATSim scenarios most often report mode share and link counts, and trip length distributions where a survey supports them - Open Berlin and the Munich comparison do, most do not.
factors.query: Whether any agent-based city model publishes a coincidence ratio for its trip length frequency distribution, and what value it reached

factors.factor: Flow-capacity, storage-capacity and stuck-time correction at a sample fraction
factors.what_research_says: The correction rules for a downscaled run are contested and were measured again this year. Mersini and Ziemke (MUM 2025, TU Berlin) set out the position: former recommendations scaled storage less than flow, flowCapacityFactor = sample share and storageCapacityFactor = sample share^alpha with alpha = 0.75 'to prevent breakdowns in small samples', while 'more recently, flow and storage capacities are usually scaled equally, i.e., with alpha = 1', the Open Berlin practice; Llorca and Moeckel found 'no substantial differences in average travel times for a given MATSim scenario when comparing different sample shares using both alpha values', and Ben-Dor, Ben-Elia and Benenson again recommend 0.75. Their measured result on a 100 per cent Lausitz benchmark is that scores and travel times are close to the full-scale run at 25 and 50 per cent, deviate at 5 per cent and clearly at 1 per cent, and that 'even average statistics (such as score and travel time) become unreliable when sampling below 10%'. The sharper finding is on the third parameter nobody scales: stuck-time violations, normalised by the inverse sample share, rise from about 40,000 at 100 per cent (about one agent in eight stuck once per day) to three times as many at 1 per cent, and with equal scaling of flow and storage 'even more than four and a half times as many' - so alpha = 1 costs stuck agents at small samples, and the paper flags that stuck time itself should be scaled with the sample size, larger for smaller samples.
factors.magnitude: literature: flowCapacityFactor = sample share; storageCapacityFactor = sample share^alpha with alpha between 0.75 and 1.0, alpha = 1 the current mainstream; at alpha = 1 stuck-time violations rise to about 4.5x the full-scale rate at a 1 per cent sample and about 3x at equal-alpha 0.75; averages unreliable below a 10 per cent sample; 25 per cent close to full scale
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim scales both capacity factors with the sample and MATSim's own GlobalConfigGroup refuses a storage factor that differs from the flow factor by more than global.relativeTolerance; SUMO and BEAM scale link capacities with the sample; the field's usual sample is 1-10 per cent and 25 per cent sits at the high end of published scenarios.
factors.query: The completed version of Mersini and Ziemke's stuck-time scaling runs - a recommended stuck-time value as a function of sample share for MATSim

factors.factor: Expanding a sampled run's link volumes for a counts comparison
factors.what_research_says: A downscaled run's link volumes must be multiplied back before they mean anything against an observed count, and MATSim carries the factor as a first-class setting: countsScaleFactor 'represents a multiplier for scaling model results back to real-world volumes, so that when a model is based on a countsScaleFactor of 10, the real fleet sizes would be ten times higher'. The expansion is only the first of three basis decisions, and the other two are where practice models put their error bars: WHICH simulated vehicles count (the observed detector counts every vehicle class, so the modelled side must either add its heavy vehicles or the observed side must be converted to a light-vehicle basis - one or the other, never neither), and WHICH link a station maps to (a two-way station is the sum of both directions and a station matched to a service road or the wrong carriageway reads near zero). The tolerance guidance is by volume class rather than per link, and the manuals warn against reading it as a standard: 'the guidelines in this section should not be construed as standards; matching or exceeding the guidelines is not sufficient to determine the validity of a model.'
factors.magnitude: literature: modelled volumes multiplied by 1/sample fraction (MATSim countsScaleFactor); tolerances by facility class rather than per link - VMT within 7-15 per cent, screenlines 5 per cent, cutlines 10 per cent; %RMSE summarised by facility type or volume group, never by single link
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim's counts module applies countsScaleFactor and plots hourly modelled against counted volumes per link; regional four-step models compare screenlines and cutlines and report %RMSE by volume group; ActivitySim hands assignment to a separate step whose counts validation follows the same manuals.
factors.query: A published agent-based scenario's counts validation that reports how many stations modelled zero and why - the failure mode of station-to-link matching rather than the aggregate %RMSE
